property_summary: After a deposit of value v into an account whose prior balance is b and where b+v would overflow uint256, the contract prevents the deposit (i.e., the deposit call reverts), so the account balance never increases when an overflow would occur.
A deposit call never reverts when the provided deposit amount is strictly less than 2**256 minus the caller's prior balance (i.e., it only reverts if adding amount would overflow).
Any single deposit that would cause the caller's balance to wrap (i.e. b + v < b) is rejected (deposit call reverts).
If deposit would overflow the caller's stored balance (i.e. b + v < b), the deposit call reverts (deposit does not complete).
Depositing an amount that would cause the caller's stored balance to wrap around is rejected (deposit call reverts).

For any depositor and any positive deposit value, calling deposit() always strictly increases that depositor's recorded balance by the sent amount (i.e., balances[msg.sender] after == before + msg.value); the mutant removed the overflow-protecting assert allowing an overflow that can make the stored balance not increase as expected.

For any depositor and any sent value, calling deposit() on the correct contract never decreases the recorded balance (i.e., balances[depositor] after the call is >= balances[depositor] before the call); the mutant removes the overflow assert allowing an overflow that can make the stored balance wrap and thus become less than before for some inputs.

For any depositor address and any uint256 value, if the depositor's prior recorded balance + msg.value does not overflow (i.e., prior + value >= prior), then after deposit() the recorded balance equals prior + value; the mutant, by removing the overflow check, allows the stored balance to differ when addition would overflow, so there exist inputs (prior balance and value causing wrap) where the mutant violates this equality.

For any depositor and any deposit value, the reference contract never lets a deposit call revert; in particular, calling deposit() always succeeds (returns/does not revert) for all msg.value and sender combinations — the mutant removes the overflow check which can cause an arithmetic overflow elsewhere and may make some calls panic, so there exist inputs where the mutant causes a revert while the reference never does.

For any depositor and any sent value, if the depositor's prior recorded balance is not the maximum uint256 (i.e., balances[depositor] < type(uint256).max), then after deposit() the recorded balance strictly increases (new balance > old balance); the mutant removing the overflow-protecting assert allows adding msg.value when prior is already max to wrap or remain equal, violating this rule for some inputs.
After calling deposit with value v, the contract's balance increases by exactly v (address(c).balance == prior + v).
